newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S. Korea raises heat on unions, rejects TV debate.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea raises heat on unions, rejects TV debate.

text.p: Riot police tightened their siege of a Seoul cathedral on Friday as one of the strike leaders hiding there made a dramatic bid by for a public debate with a senior ruling party politician but was swiftly slapped down.

Kwon Young-kil took up the ruling party's offer of a televised debate on a new labour law that has triggered widespread worker unrest, and stipulated that party chairman Lee Hong-koo must present himself at television studios.
Kwon also said the government must guarantee his safety from arrest, but the New Korea Party swiftly dismissed the offer on the grounds that he was a fugitive.
"Even for a television debate, the law should be observed," a New Korea Party statement said. "There cannot be guarantees of safety for people who have legal problems."

Police stepped up pressure on Kwon and six deputies of his Korean Confederation of Trade Unions sheltering at Myongdong cathedral, from where they have been leading more than three weeks of strikes against a new labour law.
Riot police checked cars approaching the church, peering into passenger windows and opening trunks, apparently to stop union activists slipping in or out.
But the strikes have wound down and there are now just pockets of worker resistance.

The labour ministry said strikes were tapering off, with only 57,320 workers at 48 companies involved. The confederation put the figure at up to 200,000 and vowed to continue partial strikes in public services and manufacturing.
Seoul stocks fell 2.08 percent to 697.044 points in afternoon trade on Friday on profit-taking, brokers said. They said the industrial unrest had been fully discounted by the market.
The ruling party statement rejecting Kwon's debate offer urged the confederation to put forward suitable candidates.
Kwon had insisted a debate did not imply his union was seeking dialogue over the law, which allows companies to lay off workers, replace strikers and extend work hours.
Wrangling over the debate indicated both sides were jockeying for position in a battle for public opinion.

Public support for the government is wavering, with many commentators comparing President Kim Young-sam to past strongman rulers for the way legislation that transforms South Korea's industrial landscape was rammed through.
The law was passed in a dawn sitting of parliament on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
A tough and inflexible posture on the bill has cost the government sympathy at home and triggered opposition by world labour organisations.

In what is widely viewed as an ominous warning of a crackdown, authorities have linked labour strife to North Korea and produced Communist propaganda from Pyongyang they say is circulating among strikers.
The two Koreas have been technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.

International labour organisations have stepped up their pressure on South Korea to dump the law, which they maintain curbs worker rights to freedom of association by allowing the Federation of Korean Trade Unions to retain its monopoly on union representation until 2000.
Ten leaders of trade union organisations from around the world are to due to arrive next week to replace four others who left on Thursday.
South Korea's immigration chief said the 10 would be allowed in, but warned they would be deported if they took part in strike-related protests.
